tagline.text: Laguna's first stone church, a 1600 legacy in the embroidery town of Lumban

location.label: Location
location.text: J.P. Rizal Street, Lumban town center, Laguna

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (September's Burdang Lumban Festival recommended)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~2,000 (one day from Manila, transport and meals included, embroidery shopping excluded)

children.text: San Sebastian Parish Church in Lumban was completed in 1600 and is regarded as the first stone church in Laguna, a Franciscan heritage site with a three-story facade and an octagonal bell tower. The church sits in Lumban, known as the embroidery capital of the Philippines, so it pairs well with a visit to the barong tagalog workshops.
Lumban is a small town in Laguna about
94 km
southeast of Manila and about
7 km

from Santa Cruz. San Sebastian Parish Church, in the heart of town, is counted among the oldest stone churches in Laguna. Both Wikipedia and the historical marker that the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) put up in 1939 say that after the earlier wood-and-thatch church on this site burned down, Laguna's first stone church was completed in

The history goes back to the late 16th century. The Franciscan missionary Juan de Plasencia began preaching in this area in 1578, and the first church was a temporary building of nipa and bamboo. According to the marker, that wooden church burned down and was rebuilt in stone. Many sources give 1586 as the year of the fire, but dates vary slightly between sources, so it is best to confirm the exact year with a notice inside the church or at the parish office. On October 9, 1600, the first Eucharistic procession outside Manila was held here, and in 1606 the Franciscans reportedly founded the country's first church music school on the site. During the same period the church also served as an infirmary for sick Franciscan missionaries.

The exterior can be summed up as a three-tiered facade and an octagonal bell tower standing to the right of the building. The tower has a square base with three octagonal levels, topped by a statue of St. Sebastian. The church was badly damaged in the 1880 Luzon earthquakes and restored in 1889 by Father Manuel Rodriguez. Its present form is said to date from the American period, when it was called the largest stone church in Laguna. It is also said to have been heavily damaged again by wartime destruction around 1941 and by a storm in 1947, so the building you see is the result of several restorations. A 2025 academic paper (ScienceDirect) argues that the calado carving patterns on the front doorway resemble Lumban's embroidery patterns. That reading is interpretive, but knowing this is an embroidery town's church makes the facade more interesting to look at.

Lumban is worth more than a quick look at the church. The historical marker spells the town's name as Lumbang. The town is called the "embroidery capital of the Philippines." Artisans hand-embroider fine fabrics such as piña and jusi to make traditional garments like the barong tagalog and the saya, and shops in town let you browse embroidered barongs and cloth. Around the third week of September every year, the Burdang Lumban Festival features a street dance competition by students in embroidered costumes. Whether the church is the starting point or center of the festival parade varies from year to year, so check the schedule. Combine the church and embroidery with nearby Pagsanjan Falls or Lake Caliraya for a full day trip in Laguna.

Completed in 1600, the church is described on the NHCP marker as the first stone church in Laguna. Up close, the thick stone walls and the old stonework give you a real sense of a building that has stood for more than 400 years.

blocks.title: Three-story facade and carved calado door

children.text: The facade rises in three tiers, and the doorway has delicate carving that recalls calado, an embroidery technique of making patterns by pulling out threads. Photos come out best when morning light falls on the front.
The three-level octagonal bell tower to the right of the church is topped by a statue of St. Sebastian. It is fun to compare with other Spanish-era bell towers in Laguna.

The marker installed in 1939 is on the right side of the main entrance on the facade. Its inscription says Lumbang was once the center of missionary activity in Laguna, which sums up the town's history at a glance.

blocks.title: Site of the first Eucharistic procession outside Manila

children.text: The first Eucharistic procession outside Manila is said to have been held here on October 9, 1600. The site is meaningful for Catholics and, for everyone else, a clue to how Catholicism spread in the Philippines.

Lumban's town center has several shops and workshops selling embroidered barongs and cloth. You can see calado work up close, where threads are pulled out and re-embroidered, and some places take custom orders, so ask each shop for prices directly.

Held around the third week of September, this embroidery festival features students in embroidered costumes dancing in the streets, plus embroidery contests and exhibits. The town is liveliest during this time.

The church pairs well with Laguna's eastern heritage towns such as Pagsanjan, Liliw and Pila in a single day. The Lumban parish belongs to the same parish area as Pagsanjan, Luisiana and Cavinti, so you can link them in a church-visiting itinerary. During Holy Week it is sometimes listed among Laguna's Visita Iglesia churches.
Arrive in Lumban town and start in front of San Sebastian Church on J.P. Rizal Street, looking at the facade and the bell tower.
If no service is under way, go inside and quietly look around the ceiling and altar. Avoid taking photos during services.
Walk around the town near the church and browse the barong and embroidery shops. Ask about the difference between calado embroidery and piña and jusi fabrics.
Have a Laguna-style lunch at a restaurant in town. Adding a specialty dish from a nearby town is a nice touch.
Take a tricycle or jeepney toward Pagsanjan Falls or Santa Cruz to wrap up the day.

Visiting three places in one day is tight. It is also fine to skip the falls and spend the time enjoying just the church and embroidery shops.

items.title: From Manila by bus and jeepney

children.text: Take a bus bound for Santa Cruz (Laguna) from a terminal around Buendia or Ayala in Manila. The transport site Rome2rio lists the trip from One Ayala to Santa Cruz at about
2+ hours
From Santa Cruz to Lumban is about
7 km
. Transfer to a jeepney or tricycle, and check the fare locally.
Some sources say there is no direct bus from Manila to Lumban. Services change often, so confirm at the terminal.
Ride-hailing apps may not work well in rural stretches, so leave yourself plenty of time to get back.

items.title: From Manila by car or rental

children.text: Lumban is about
94 km
from Manila. Depending on traffic it can take two to three hours or more, so avoid rush hour.
Parking near the church in Lumban town may be tight, so it is easier to park at the edge of town.
In Lumban town you get around by tricycle and on foot. The church and the embroidery shops are within walking distance of each other.
To reach Pagsanjan or Lake Caliraya, charter a tricycle or transfer to a jeepney. Negotiate the fare and confirm it before boarding.
Because you can visit the church both inside and out, the dry season from November to May is the most comfortable. Early morning is best for avoiding the midday heat.

Around the third week of September, the Burdang Lumban Festival brings a parade of embroidered costumes. January 20 is the feast day of the church's patron, St. Sebastian, with parish events. Catholic traditions center on Mass and processions, so even as a sightseer, watch quietly and do not disrupt the proceedings.

Lumban is a day-trip destination, and there are not many large hotels in town. If you want to stay overnight, the towns of Santa Cruz and Pagsanjan offer more choices. Lake Caliraya has resorts and vacation homes, so if you want to combine the lake with your visit, stay there. Prices vary widely by season, so check on booking sites.

Most visitors have lunch at a local eatery in town or from street food. Laguna brings to mind sweets such as buko pie and kusu, but ask locally which shops are in Lumban. We have not listed specific shop names because none could be verified, so ask locals for recommendations.
It is polite not to tour the church during services. Check the Mass schedule with the parish in advance.
Modest clothing that covers the shoulders and knees is best.
If you want to buy an embroidered barong, be sure to ask about the fabric (piña, jusi or other) and the embroidery method (machine or hand). Hand embroidery takes a long time and costs more.
Custom orders can take from a few days to several weeks, so confirm the schedule.
The dates of the September festival change every year, so check with the Lumban municipal tourism office. The festival's Facebook page lists the tourism office's contact details.
Bring plenty of cash. Small shops may not accept cards.
For photos, the facade looks best in morning light, and you need to step back to fit the whole bell tower in the frame.
During big events such as Holy Week, the town gets crowded, so arrive early.
The church is an active parish where services are held. Access may be limited during Mass and events, so please behave quietly.
We could not confirm the Mass schedule or visiting hours. Check with the parish office or locally.
There may be no direct public transport from Manila, so check the last return departure in advance.
During the rainy and typhoon seasons, parts of Laguna can flood, so check the weather forecast.
Confirm prices precisely at embroidery shops and get a receipt.
Watch out for pickpockets and keep valuables on your person.
